3.2 — Projectiles: Instantiate, Fire, Destroy

Your turret knows when you are near; now it needs teeth. This is the lesson where the course stops holding your hand: everything a projectile needs, you have already written once, somewhere else. Your job today is to recognise that — and then prove it.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I shoot a projectile?”Solo build
Break It Down~10 minSolo build

A turret that shoots at me. That is the whole feature, and it is far too big to hold in your head at once — which is exactly why every lesson in this course starts the same way.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

No parts listed here on purpose. Splitting the problem up is the work of this lesson — write your list before you open the file.

Notice what is NOT on that list: no new API except the spawner, and even that you have seen. Five parts, four of them lifted straight out of lessons you have already finished. That is what a well-sequenced course feels like from the inside — not "here is a new thing you have never seen", but "here is the same five things, pointed at a new target".

The test for a finished split: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make the turret shoot" cannot be looked up. "Clone a prefab at a position" can. If a part is still too big to search for, it is two parts.

Your turn

List the parts of this problem, in the order you would build them.

There is more than one way to make the bullet travel. Name two, say what each one costs you in components, and say which you picked and why.

The Problem ~10 min

No specification this time, and no API table. You have earned the version of this lesson where you are handed the behaviour and nothing else. Here is what the finished feature does, from the player's seat:

  1. I walk into the turret's range, and something appears at the end of the barrel — not at the turret's centre, and not at the world origin.
  2. It flies toward where I was standing when it was fired. If I keep moving, it does not follow me — it commits to the shot it took.
  3. It travels at the same speed whether I am standing next to the turret or at the far edge of its range.
  4. It cleans itself up a few seconds later if it hits nothing.

Read those four again with your list of parts next to them. Every one of them is a part you named, and every one of them is testable by playing the game — which is the other half of breaking a problem down. A part you cannot test is not a part yet.

Architectural constraint (the only thing I will hand you): you are editing two files, and they do not know about each other's details. TurretController.cs decides when to fire and where the bullet starts. Projectile.cs owns everything about the bullet after that: which way it goes, how fast, and when it dies. If you find yourself writing the bullet's speed into the turret, stop — the turret should not know that number exists.
Build Lab: Alone ~35 min

Open Assets/Prefabs/Turret_Projectile. You will find an empty Projectile component already attached — the same pattern as the turret and the coin. Nothing new needs creating. Fill it in, then extend the range check you wrote in 3.1 so it fires.

When you are stuck, this is the order to reread:

  1. 2.4 — prefabs, and cloning one at runtime
  2. 2.1 — the whole pickup pattern, including the destroy
  3. 1.5 — vectors and normalizing, where the diagonal bug was fixed
  4. 2.2 — your movement line, and why velocity takes no deltaTime
  5. 3.1 — the range check you are extending
  6. Unity + C# Quick Reference — when you know the name and need the exact spelling

That list is the point of the lesson. When you have forgotten how to clone something, you do not ask a person and you do not guess — you go and read the lesson where you already did it. A working programmer spends most of the day reading, and this list is what "reading the documentation for each part" looks like when the documentation is your own course.

Wire the slots before you press Play. An unassigned prefab or muzzle slot does not complain at startup — it throws at the exact moment you step into range, which looks like a firing bug and is really a setup bug. Assign them, then play.

Save, wire the slots, and press Play. Walk into range: a projectile appears at the muzzle and travels. Do not celebrate the fire rate yet — you are currently firing every single frame, because your range check runs every frame. That is exactly the problem the next lesson solves.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Break a feature into parts small enough to look each one up on its own
  • Name which part of this feature was lifted from a lesson you had already done
  • Say where you would look up a Unity API you have forgotten, without asking a person
  • Explain the role of Instantiate in stamping runtime clones
  • Explain why a direction vector is normalized, and what goes wrong without it
  • Name two ways to move a projectile and state what each one costs
  • Explain why your turret currently fires every frame
  • Commit and push
